question: Why should nurses report near misses even when no patient gets hurt?

options.A: To fulfill legal requirements for police notification
options.B: To help identify system weaknesses before real injury happens
options.C: To prove that equipment failure is the main hospital problem
options.D: To ensure the nurse involved faces disciplinary action

explanation: Near misses highlight vulnerabilities in safety barriers before a tragedy of patient harm occurs. [learn more](GST319_U5_T6#GST319_U5_T6_h1)

question: In the Swiss Cheese Model of patient safety, what do the holes in the cheese slices represent?
explanation: Each slice of cheese has holes, which symbolize flaws or gaps in hospital safety protocols and barriers. [learn more](GST319_U5_T6#GST319_U5_T6_h2)

question: According to the Swiss Cheese Model, when does a serious medical error finally reach the patient?

options.A: When equipment is purchased from unlicensed vendors
options.B: When holes in multiple defense layers line up
options.C: When a single nurse makes a minor calculation error
options.D: When hospital management ignores patient complaints

explanation: A hazard only reaches the patient when the vulnerabilities in all independent safety barriers align simultaneously. [learn more](GST319_U5_T6#GST319_U5_T6_h2)

question: Which of these is a clear example of an active failure by frontline staff?

options.A: A nurse giving the wrong medication dose
options.B: Chronic understaffing on a surgical ward
options.C: A poorly designed automated dispensing cabinet
options.D: Confusing label designs on IV fluid bags

explanation: Active failures are unsafe acts committed by frontline personnel who are directly interacting with patients. [learn more](GST319_U5_T6#GST319_U5_T6_h3)

question: Why are latent conditions often considered more dangerous than active failures?

options.A: They cannot be prevented by any hospital safety committee
options.B: They remain hidden in the system until triggered by circumstances
options.C: They can only be corrected by government health ministries
options.D: They immediately result in patient death without warning signs

explanation: Latent conditions sit quietly in the background of daily operations until an unsuspecting worker interacts with them. [learn more](GST319_U5_T6#GST319_U5_T6_h3)

question: What is the proper management response to an honest human error within a just culture?

options.A: Assign mandatory overtime shifts as a penalty
options.B: Console the worker and review the process
options.C: File a formal police report for negligence
options.D: Suspend the nursing license immediately without inquiry

explanation: Human errors are inadvertent slips, so the proper response involves supporting the staff and fixing the broken process. [learn more](GST319_U5_T6#GST319_U5_T6_h4)

question: How does a just culture differ from a traditional blame culture in nursing?

options.A: It places total legal responsibility on the hospital director
options.B: It ignores all medication errors to keep staff morale high
options.C: It eliminates the need for written incident reports
options.D: It looks at system flaws instead of automatically punishing individuals

explanation: A just culture balances individual accountability with the understanding that system design heavily influences human action. [learn more](GST319_U5_T6#GST319_U5_T6_h4)

question: What is the main goal of conducting a Root Cause Analysis after an adverse event?

options.A: To find the underlying system factors that caused the incident
options.B: To fulfill mandatory paperwork for international accreditation bodies
options.C: To determine which staff member should be fired for negligence
options.D: To gather legal evidence to protect the hospital from lawsuits

explanation: Root Cause Analysis looks deep into the process to uncover foundational system failures rather than just blaming individuals. [learn more](GST319_U5_T6#GST319_U5_T6_h5)

question: Why might a nurse hesitate to use a hospital incident reporting system?

options.A: Rule that only doctors are allowed to document errors
options.B: Lack of interest in improving patient outcomes
options.C: Fear of disciplinary action or negative repercussions
options.D: Belief that computers are too difficult to operate

explanation: Punitive environments discourage transparent reporting, causing many errors to remain undocumented and unaddressed. [learn more](GST319_U5_T6#GST319_U5_T6_h5)

question: Why are system-level changes more effective than simply telling nurses to be more careful?

options.A: Technology completely eliminates the possibility of human presence
options.B: Humans naturally make errors when relying solely on memory and attention
options.C: Written guidelines are legally binding in all Nigerian courts
options.D: Staff members usually ignore verbal warnings from nursing management

explanation: System changes like checklists and automated safeguards compensate for normal human limitations in memory and focus. [learn more](GST319_U5_T6#GST319_U5_T6_h6)

question: A ward has repeated wrong-dose errors because two drug packages look very similar. What is the best system-level fix?

options.A: Warn all nurses to read the drug labels three times before opening
options.B: Store the medications in separate, clearly labeled locations
options.C: Issue written reprimands to the nurses who made the administration slips
options.D: Remove the medication from the hospital formulary completely

explanation: Separating look-alike packaging physically alters the environment to prevent active administration failures. [learn more](GST319_U5_T6#GST319_U5_T6_h6)
